title: Rhythm Guitar Basics
goal: Play a full rhythm part through a whole song: steady pulse, chord changes in time, strum patterns and dynamics.

steps.title: Feel the pulse before you play
steps.description:
[Before you start]
This roadmap assumes you can tune your guitar, hold a pick and fret at least two open chords (E minor and A minor are enough), even slowly. No previous rhythm training is needed. By the end you will play a complete rhythm part through a whole song: a steady pulse, chord changes in time, strum patterns with rests, accents and muting, and a performance you can record and play with other people.

[What it is]
The pulse is the steady, evenly spaced beat that every rhythm part sits on. Before touching the guitar you learn to keep it in your body: tap a foot, clap or nod with a metronome, then keep going when the click stops.

[Why it matters]
Everything later in this roadmap (strums, chord changes, rests, syncopation) is placed relative to this beat. If the beat lives only in the metronome and not in you, every rest and every chord change will drift. Good rhythm players predict the beat instead of reacting to it, and that prediction is trained here.

[How to practice]
Set a metronome between 60 and 80 BPM and clap or tap on every click for a minute. Aim to land exactly with the click so the two sounds merge into one. Then use the Metronome Gap Test: the click plays for two bars, goes silent, and you tap the next downbeat. Watch the deviation reading and try to centre it on zero across several attempts. Finish by tapping along to any song you like and finding beat one of every bar.
steps.successCriteria: You can clap with a metronome at 60–80 BPM for 16 beats with tap and click merging into one sound, and in the Metronome Gap Test you land within about 50 ms of the downbeat on three attempts in a row. You can tap beat one of every bar along with a recording you have never played to.

lessons.title: Using a Metronome | Beginner Guitar Tips

steps.title: Quarter-note downstrokes
steps.description:
[What it is]
One even downstroke per beat across the strings, with the fretting hand holding a single easy chord (E minor) or lightly muting the strings. Four strums per bar, every strum landing on the click.

[Why it matters]
The downstroke on the beat is the most common motion in rhythm guitar and the baseline for every pattern that follows. Freddie Green held the Count Basie band together for decades with four quarter-note strums per bar, and Malcolm Young built AC/DC riffs from downstrokes. If your quarter notes are even in volume and timing, everything else gets easier; if they are not, more complex patterns hide the problem instead of fixing it.

[How to practice]
Hold E minor, set the metronome to 60 BPM and play one downstroke per click. Work on three things: the motion comes from a relaxed wrist and forearm, not the shoulder; the pick hits the same strings from the same depth every time; every strum has the same volume. Play four bars, rest, repeat. Record 30 seconds and listen for strums that stick out as louder, quieter or late. Raise the tempo to 70 and 80 only once a tempo feels effortless for two minutes.
steps.successCriteria: A 30-second recording of quarter-note downstrokes on E minor at 60–80 BPM sounds even: no strum is noticeably louder, quieter or off the click. Your wrist and forearm stay loose after two minutes.

lessons.title: Basic Downstroke and Upstroke Technique for Rhythm Strumming

steps.title: Count out loud and find beat one
steps.description:
[What it is]
Saying "1, 2, 3, 4" out loud while you play, so you always know which beat you are on and where the bar starts. On the guitar this means strumming quarter notes on one chord while counting, and later counting through a chord change without the count hesitating.

[Why it matters]
Counting is how you find your place when something goes wrong, how you learn a pattern from a chart, and how you talk to other musicians about rhythm. Beat one is the anchor: chord changes, section changes and most accents are organised around it. Players who lose beat one lose the band.

[How to practice]
Strum quarter notes on E minor at 60–70 BPM and say each beat number as you strum it, slightly louder on "1". If speaking breaks your strumming, slow down until both happen together. Then put a rest on beat 3 and an accent on beat 1, and keep saying every number out loud, including the one you are not playing. Finally count "1, 2, 3, 4" through a change from E minor to A minor every bar: the count must not pause while your fingers move.
steps.successCriteria: You can strum quarter notes while counting "1, 2, 3, 4" aloud in time with the click for two minutes, including a chord change every bar, without the count or the strum stopping. You can point to beat one in any bar of a recording you are listening to.

lessons.title: Strumming: How to Practice Counting the Beats | Guitar for Beginners
How To Count Rhythm on Guitar for Beginners

steps.title: Rests, long notes and clean stops
steps.description:
[What it is]
Playing silence on purpose. A half note is a strum that rings for two beats, a whole note for four, and a rest is a beat where you stop the strings and play nothing. Stopping means resting the side of your picking hand on the strings, or relaxing the fretting fingers, exactly on the beat.

[Why it matters]
Rhythm guitar is as much about where sound ends as where it starts. Malcolm Young's AC/DC parts are famous for the space between chords, and a band relies on the rhythm guitarist to define that space. Rests also make every pattern later in the roadmap possible: a strum pattern is just a choice of which beats sound and which are silent.

[How to practice]
Hold E minor and count "1, 2, 3, 4" aloud. Play this sequence: a bar of four quarter notes; a bar of two half notes (strum on 1 and 3, let them ring); a whole note (strum on 1, let it ring for the bar); a bar with a strum on 1 followed by three counted rests. Stop the strings dead on the rest, no lingering ring, and re-enter exactly on the next downbeat. Then play Rhythm Training — Easy, which mixes quarter notes, half notes and rests on a muted string and checks your timing. Vary it: stop on beat 3, play two bars and rest one.
steps.successCriteria: You can loop a bar of quarter notes, a bar of half notes, a whole note and a bar with counted rests at 60–80 BPM without losing the count. Every stop is silent instantly, and every re-entry lands on the intended beat.

lessons.title: Guitar Rhythm theory - Rests - Whole, Half, Quarter and Eighth Notes
Reading Music on Guitar - Note and Rest Values made EASY!

steps.title: Essential open chords, ringing clean
steps.description:
[What it is]
The open chords that carry most beginner songs: E minor, A minor, D, A, E, C and G. The goal here is not speed but sound: every string that should ring, rings; every string that should be silent, is silent.

[Why it matters]
These seven shapes are enough to accompany hundreds of songs, but only if they ring clean. A buzzing or dead string spoils a rhythm part even when the timing is perfect, and you cannot fix chord sound later while also thinking about a strum pattern. This is the moment to build the habit.

[How to practice]
Learn two or three shapes at a time in Chord Practice — Pick Your Chords. For each shape, place the fingers, then pick the strings one at a time and listen. Fix a buzz by moving the fingertip closer to the fret wire or arching the finger more; fix a dead string by checking whether a neighbouring finger is touching it. Keep the thumb behind the neck, roughly opposite the middle finger, so the fingers can curl. Once a chord rings clean, strum eight quarter notes on it and check that it stays clean. Only then add the next shape.
steps.successCriteria: You can form all seven chords (Em, Am, D, A, E, C, G) so that a string-by-string check produces no buzz or dead note, and you can strum eight quarter notes on any of them without the sound degrading. The hand looks relaxed and the thumb stays behind the neck.

lessons.title: (Part1) 11 Basic Guitar Chords that every Beginner Guitarist should know ~ Open Major & Minor Chords
Are You Doing It Wrong? Correct Thumb Placement for Guitar

steps.title: Two-chord changes on the beat
steps.description:
[What it is]
Switching between two open chords while the quarter-note strum keeps going, so that the first strum on the new chord lands on beat one and sounds as clean as the others.

[Why it matters]
Chord changes are where beginners lose the beat: the fretting hand takes too long, so the strum arrives late or hits a half-formed chord. A rhythm part that pauses at every change is not usable in a song. Being able to change on the beat is the single most important accompaniment skill.

[How to practice]
Pick an easy pair (Em to Am, Am to C, G to Em, D to A). At 60 BPM, play four quarter-note strums on the first chord and four on the second, in a loop. Start moving the fingers as you play beat 4 so the shape is ready on beat 1. If the first strum after the change is late or dirty, slow down rather than stopping. Add JustinGuitar's One Minute Changes drill: for one minute, change back and forth between the two chords as many times as you can, count the clean changes, and write the number down each session.
steps.successCriteria: You can loop two chords with quarter-note strums at 60–70 BPM for two minutes where the first strum after every change is clean and on the click. In One Minute Changes you reach at least 30 clean changes for two different pairs.

lessons.title: Get Strumming & Chord Changes Right! | Guitar for Beginners
Chord Switching Practice - C to G

steps.title: Change without stopping the strum
steps.description:
[What it is]
Two habits that keep the strum going through a change. A pivot finger is a finger that stays on the same string and fret in both chords (the first finger between C and Am, the third finger between G and Em with the right fingering), so fewer fingers move. An air change means the last strum of the bar is played while the fingers are already lifting, so the strumming hand never waits for the fretting hand.

[Why it matters]
Wasted motion is what makes changes slow, and a stopped strumming hand is what makes them audible. Moving fewer fingers a shorter distance, and letting the last strum of the bar be slightly open, is how experienced players change chords at song tempos without a gap.

[How to practice]
For each pair you know, say aloud which fingers stay and which move, then practise the change in slow motion keeping the moving fingers within a centimetre of the strings. Then loop the pair with quarter notes and let the strum on beat 4 catch the strings as the fingers lift; the strum on beat 1 must land on the full new chord. Film your fretting hand from above and look for fingers flying up. Use Chord Practice — Pick Your Chords with the pair at 60–80 BPM.
steps.successCriteria: For your five most common pairs you can name the pivot fingers, and a video of your hand shows no finger rising more than about a centimetre during the change. You can loop each pair at 80 BPM with quarter notes and no gap in the strumming.

lessons.title: Strings Ringing Out Between Chord Changes

steps.title: Four-chord loops from real songs
steps.description:
[What it is]
Playing progressions of three or four chords in a loop without stopping: G, D, Em, C (I–V–vi–IV in G); C, G, Am, F (with an easy F such as Fmaj7); Am, C, G, D; and the 12-bar blues in A (A, D, E). One bar of quarter notes per chord first, then two beats per chord.

[Why it matters]
Most popular songs cycle through a few chords. Hooktheory's analysis of 1,300 popular songs found the move from I to V to be the most common change, and the I–V–vi–IV loop is the famous "four-chord song"; JustinGuitar's beginner song lists are built on the same loops. Once a four-chord loop runs without stopping, you can accompany a real song from beginning to end. The loop also trains anticipation: while playing one chord you already think of the next.

[How to practice]
Write the progression on paper. At 60 BPM play one bar of quarter notes per chord and loop it. Keep the beat even if a change is rough, then clean up the weakest change with One Minute Changes. When a loop is solid at one bar per chord, play two beats per chord. The hardest change is usually from the last chord back to the first; give it extra repetitions. Learn at least two loops from memory so you can look at your hands or a lyric sheet instead of the chart.
steps.successCriteria: You can play two different four-chord loops and a 12-bar blues from memory at 70 BPM, one bar and then two beats per chord, for three minutes without stopping, with every chord clean on its first strum.

lessons.title: 10 Easiest Guitar Songs Ever - ONLY 4 CHORDS (G, D, Em, C)

steps.title: Strum the right strings
steps.description:
[What it is]
Every open chord has a lowest string that should sound (the sixth for E, Em and G; the fifth for A, Am and C; the fourth for D) and strings that should stay silent. This step is about starting the strum on the right string and keeping the unwanted ones quiet, either by not hitting them or by muting them with the fretting hand.

[Why it matters]
The lowest note defines the chord. A D chord with the open low E ringing sounds like a different, muddy chord, and a C with the sixth string open loses its bass. Controlling which strings sound is also the first step towards bass-strum patterns and the percussive muting later in the roadmap.

[How to practice]
For each chord, name its bass string and pluck it alone, then strum the rest. Aim the downstroke to start from that string; for D and C, let the tip of the thumb or the side of a fretting finger lightly touch the strings above the bass note so they stay silent even if the pick brushes them. Use Muting — Inside a D Chord to practise silencing individual strings by relaxing a finger without lifting it. Test yourself by recording a slow strum of each chord and listening for a wrong low note.
steps.successCriteria: For all seven open chords you can name the bass string and, in a recording of slow strums, no wrong low string is audible. You can hold a D chord and keep the fifth and sixth strings silent while strumming across all six strings.

lessons.title: How to stop buzzing and muting guitar strings?

steps.title: The eighth-note pendulum
steps.description:
[What it is]
Splitting each beat in two: a downstroke on the number ("1, 2, 3, 4") and an upstroke on the "and". The hand swings like a pendulum, down on the beat and up between beats, and it keeps swinging even when a stroke is later skipped.

[Why it matters]
Almost every strum pattern in pop, rock, folk and country is a selection of strokes from this continuous down-up motion. If the pendulum is steady, learning a new pattern is just deciding which strokes miss the strings. If the pendulum stops and starts, every pattern has to be learned from scratch, and the timing wobbles.

[How to practice]
Hold one chord at 60 BPM, count "1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and" aloud and play down on the numbers and up on the "ands". Keep the upstroke lighter and shallower; it usually catches only the three or four thinnest strings, which is fine. Play Strumming — Down-Up and listen for even spacing between down and up. Then keep the motion going through a chord change: the hand does not wait for the fingers.
steps.successCriteria: You can strum continuous eighth notes at 60–80 BPM for two minutes with even spacing between down and up strokes, counting aloud, and keep the motion unbroken through a chord change every bar.

lessons.title: Basic Downstroke and Upstroke Technique for Rhythm Strumming

steps.title: Your first patterns: add the upstroke
steps.description:
[What it is]
Turning the pendulum into a pattern by letting some strokes miss the strings. The first pattern is four downstrokes with a single upstroke on the "and" of 4 (D D D DU). Next comes D DU D DU, where the upstrokes after beats 2 and 4 are played.

[Why it matters]
This is the mechanism behind every pattern you will ever learn: the arm keeps its eighth-note swing, and you choose which strokes touch the strings. The first patterns also sound like real songs immediately, so you can accompany a two-chord tune at the end of this step.

[How to practice]
Say the pattern before playing it ("down, down, down, down-up"), tapping it on your leg. Play it on muted strings, then on one chord, then over a two-chord loop. The rule that matters: on a missed stroke the arm still moves, it just passes above the strings. Use Strumming 2 — Downs + Final Up at 60–70 BPM until the upstroke lands exactly on the "and" of 4 and is lighter than the downstrokes. Then try D DU D DU the same way.
steps.successCriteria: You can play D D D DU and D DU D DU over a two-chord loop at 60–80 BPM for two minutes with the arm swinging continuously, the upstrokes lighter than the downstrokes, and no stroke landing off the count.

lessons.title: Easy Strumming Patterns With Up Strums | Guitar for Beginners
3 Essential Strumming Patterns - Beginner Guitar Lessons

steps.title: Count and read strum patterns
steps.description:
[What it is]
Reading a pattern written as counts and arrows (D on 1, D on 2, DU on 3, DU on 4) and playing it correctly the first time; and the reverse, hearing a pattern and writing it down. You count "1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and" and know on which syllable each stroke falls.

[Why it matters]
A pattern learned only by copying cannot be fixed when it goes wrong and cannot be learned from a chart or a lesson video without endless rewinding. Counting turns patterns into something you understand, which is also how you will later write your own pattern for a song.

[How to practice]
Take a pattern you know and count it aloud, saying which counts sound and which are missed. Then open Strumming 9 — Skip First & (D, DU, DU, DU) and learn it from the chart alone: count it, tap it, then play it on a chord at 60 BPM. Next, listen to the strumming in three songs you like and write down what you hear as counts and arrows, then check by playing along. Keep a page of patterns you have written down.
steps.successCriteria: Given a written pattern of eight eighth-note positions you can play it correctly within a minute at 60–70 BPM. Given a recording of a simply strummed song you can write down its main pattern and play along with it.

lessons.title: How to Read Strumming Notation
7 Tips for Reading Strumming Patterns

steps.title: THE pattern: D DU UDU
steps.description:
[What it is]
The pattern that fits more songs than any other: down on 1, down-up on 2, up on the "and" of 3, down-up on 4 (D, DU, U, DU). JustinGuitar calls it "Old Faithful". The new element is the missed downstroke on beat 3: the arm swings down past the strings, and the upstroke on the "and" is the only sound on that beat.

[Why it matters]
This one pattern will get you through a large share of pop, folk, rock and country songs, and it contains the skill that all syncopated patterns need: skipping a downbeat while the arm keeps moving. Getting it solid now means every later pattern is a small variation rather than a new problem.

[How to practice]
Count "1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and" and say the strokes: "down, down-up, up, down-up". Tap it on your leg, then play it on muted strings, then on one chord at 60 BPM. The app's Strumming 6 — Syncopated Ups is this pattern without the final upstroke (D, DU, U, D): play it as written first, then add the last up yourself. Move it over a four-chord loop at 60–80 BPM and keep the strum unbroken through the changes.
steps.successCriteria: You can play D DU UDU over a four-chord loop at 70–80 BPM for three minutes without a break in the pendulum, with the missed downstroke on beat 3 silent and the upstroke on the "and" of 3 clearly audible. You can describe the pattern in counts.

lessons.title: Why This Pattern Works for Every Song

steps.title: Rests inside a pattern
steps.description:
[What it is]
Putting a silence inside a strum pattern on purpose: the chord is stopped on a specific count and re-enters on another, while the arm keeps its swing above the strings. This combines the clean stops from the first phase with eighth-note patterns.

[Why it matters]
Patterns with rests are what make a groove breathe. The difference between a campfire strum and a part that sounds like a record is often nothing more than a well-placed stop. Rests also prepare you for the muted "chucks" and for syncopation, where hits and silences fall between the beats.

[How to practice]
Play Strumming 26 — Down-Up Pairs (DU, rest, DU, rest): a down-up on beat 1, silence on beat 2, down-up on 3, silence on 4. Stop the chord by relaxing the fretting fingers or touching the strings with the picking hand, exactly on the count, and count through the silence. Then take THE pattern and insert one rest on beat 4; record it and listen whether the rest sounds intentional. Try longer silences: play a bar, rest a bar, come back on beat 1.
steps.successCriteria: You can play patterns that contain rests on beats 2 and 4, or on the "and" of a beat, at 60–80 BPM with the silence starting exactly on the count and the arm still swinging. A listener cannot tell a rest from a mistake, because every silence sounds intended.

lessons.title: All About Musical Ties & Strumming Patterns

steps.title: Long and short: control how long a chord rings
steps.description:
[What it is]
Deciding how long each strum sustains. The same progression can be played with chords ringing into each other (legato) or with each strum cut short (staccato), and a good rhythm part mixes both on purpose.

[Why it matters]
Duration is a dimension of a rhythm part that beginners rarely control. Malcolm Young's verses are built on chords that are hit, held for exactly the right length and stopped; Freddie Green cut every quarter note short so the guitar became part of the drums. Choosing sustain per section is also how you make a verse sound calmer than a chorus with the same chords.

[How to practice]
Play Strumming 18 — Half-Time Feel (a strum on 1 and on 3) two ways: first let each chord ring the full two beats, then cut each chord after one beat by relaxing the fretting hand, and count the silence. Alternate four bars long, four bars short. Then mix within a bar: long on 1, short on 3. Do the same with THE pattern, letting the chord ring through the missed downstroke or stopping it there.
steps.successCriteria: You can play the same four-chord loop at 70 BPM in a fully ringing version and a fully staccato version, switch between them every four bars on request, and mix long and short strums within a bar with no unintended ring or early stop.

lessons.title: Strings Ringing Out Between Chord Changes

steps.title: Loud and soft: dynamics across a song
steps.description:
[What it is]
Playing the same pattern at three clearly different volumes (soft, medium, loud) by changing how deep and how fast the pick moves, not by turning a knob; then assigning volumes to sections, typically a quieter verse and a louder chorus, and moving between them without the tempo changing.

[Why it matters]
A part played at one volume sounds mechanical, and it leaves the singer no room. Dynamics are how a rhythm guitarist shapes the energy of a song and how a band builds into a chorus. JustinGuitar puts dynamics in the last module of Grade 1 for the same reason: it is what makes the beginner patterns sound like music.

[How to practice]
Play Dynamics — Soft to Loud to feel the pick moving from a shallow, light stroke to a deep, fast one. Then play THE pattern over a loop four bars soft, four medium, four loud, four medium, four soft, at a fixed 70 BPM; the rhythm must not change with the volume. Record it and check that the three levels are obviously different and the soft version still sounds like full chords. Finally play a verse-chorus form: eight bars soft, eight bars loud, twice.
steps.successCriteria: You can play THE pattern over a chord loop at 70 BPM at three volume levels that are clearly distinguishable in a recording, move between them every four bars without the tempo moving, and the softest level still produces full, clean chords.

lessons.title: Strumming Dynamics for Beginners | Transform Your Play!
HOW TO Improve Acoustic Guitar Strumming Dynamics with THIS Strumming Exercise

steps.title: Accents and the backbeat
steps.description:
[What it is]
Making chosen strums louder than the rest. The most useful accent is the backbeat: beats 2 and 4, where the drummer's snare falls. The other strums stay noticeably softer, so the accent stands out by contrast rather than by everything being loud.

[Why it matters]
Accents are what make a strum sound like a groove instead of a wall of even strokes. Rock, pop, country and R&B live on the backbeat, and a guitarist who accents 2 and 4 automatically sits together with the snare drum. Dave Isaacs' "Strumming is Drumming" lesson makes the point directly: treat the guitar as a percussion instrument and match the kick and snare.

[How to practice]
Play continuous eighth notes on one chord at 70 BPM with every stroke deliberately soft. Then hit beats 2 and 4 harder, keeping everything else soft; count aloud and say "2" and "4" louder too. Use Strumming — Rock Accents, which marks the accented strokes. Then move the accent: only beat 1, then the "and" of 2 and 4. Record each version and check that the accent is clearly louder and the others stay quiet. Put the backbeat accent into THE pattern over a chord loop.
steps.successCriteria: Playing eighth notes or THE pattern over a chord loop at 70–90 BPM, you can put a clear accent on 2 and 4 while the other strums stay soft, then move the accent to beat 1 or to the "ands" on request, and a recording shows the difference plainly.

lessons.title: How to create GROOVE in strumming - The 2 Essential Techniques

steps.title: Palm muting
steps.description:
[What it is]
Resting the fleshy edge of the picking hand on the strings right at the bridge while you strum or pick, so the notes still have pitch but ring short and thick. Moving the hand slightly towards the neck mutes more; moving it back towards the bridge lets more ring.

[Why it matters]
Palm muting gives you a third sound between open strumming and a full stop, and it is the sound of rock rhythm guitar: chugging low strings, tight verses that open up in the chorus, riffs that stay clean under distortion. Jon Finn also uses palm-muted downstrokes as a timing test, because any deviation from the click is instantly audible when the notes are short.

[How to practice]
Play Down Picking — Slow & Heavy: palm-muted downstrokes on the low E string at 60 BPM. Find the spot where the note still has pitch but no sustain; if it turns into a dull thud you are too far from the bridge, if it rings you are too far back. Keep the hand still while the wrist moves. Then apply it to a two-finger power chord (fifth fret on the low E plus seventh fret on the A) and to E minor: two bars muted, two bars open, without changing the tempo. Finally mute only beats 1 and 3 and open the strum on 2 and 4.
steps.successCriteria: You can play palm-muted eighth-note downstrokes on the low E and on a power chord at 60–90 BPM with an even, pitched chug, and switch between two bars muted and two bars open on E minor without the tempo or the hand position drifting.

lessons.title: Palm Muting | Beginner Guitar Tips
Guitar Palm Muting and Strumming 101

steps.title: Percussive chucks: the fretting hand mutes
steps.description:
[What it is]
A strum with no pitch, just a short "chk": the fretting fingers relax their pressure but stay touching the strings, and the picking hand strums normally. Placed on beats 2 and 4 it imitates the snare; placed between chord hits it fills the gaps in a pattern with rhythm instead of silence.

[Why it matters]
This is the most used percussive sound in acoustic pop, funk, reggae and R&B. Nile Rodgers built a career on "chucking": the right hand keeps strumming, the left hand decides which strokes ring and which are choked. For a beginner it solves a common problem: patterns that feel empty between chord hits, and hands that stop moving during rests.

[How to practice]
Hold a chord, strum it, then relax the fingers so the strings are damped but still touched, and strum again: chord, chk, chord, chk on quarter notes at 60 BPM. Use Muting — Inside a D Chord to practise relaxing fingers without lifting them. Then put the chuck on 2 and 4 inside a quarter-note strum, then inside THE pattern on the "and" of 2. Watch for open strings ringing when fingers lift too far, and for the fretting hand pressing again too late so the next chord is muted.
steps.successCriteria: You can play a chord loop at 70–90 BPM with a clean, unpitched chuck on beats 2 and 4 and no open strings ringing through, then insert chucks into THE pattern on the "ands" without the tempo changing, for two minutes.

lessons.title: Here's How You Get A Percussive Strumming on Guitar

steps.title: Syncopation: hits between the beats
steps.description:
[What it is]
Patterns where the important strums fall on the "ands" and some downbeats are skipped. Strumming 7 — Inside Upstrokes (DU, U, DU, U: the downstrokes on beats 2 and 4 miss) is the first one; the weight of the pattern moves off the beat while your foot and your count stay on it.

[Why it matters]
Syncopation is the ingredient that makes a rhythm part push forward instead of marching. Nearly every pop, rock and folk song has it in the strumming, and Berklee's rhythm guitar course treats syncopation as a core skill together with time-feel. It also tests your pulse: you can only play against the beat if you still feel it.

[How to practice]
Count "1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and" aloud and tap the foot on the numbers throughout. Play Strumming 7 at 60 BPM on one chord, saying the strokes; the arm keeps the pendulum, the downstrokes on 2 and 4 pass above the strings. Then try Strumming 10 — Upstroke Run and Strumming 16 — Double Down-Up from the library, always from the chart with counting. Put the one you like best over a four-chord loop with changes on beat 1.
steps.successCriteria: You can play two syncopated patterns (including Strumming 7) over a four-chord loop at 70–80 BPM for two minutes with the foot tapping steadily on the beat, the skipped downstrokes silent and the "and" strums clearly placed; you can say on which counts the strums fall.

lessons.title: Syncopation Explained for Guitar Players
Syncopated Strums Guitar Lesson with Tom Butwin

steps.title: Off-beat upstrokes: the skank
steps.description:
[What it is]
A pattern of upstrokes only, on every "and", with the downstrokes on the beats missing the strings or landing as a chuck: the reggae and ska rhythm, also used in pop verses. The downbeat is silent, so the off-beat carries the whole part.

[Why it matters]
Nothing tests your internal pulse like playing only between the beats. If you can keep a steady skank, you can keep time in any situation, and your upstrokes become as controlled as your downstrokes, which improves every other pattern. It also adds a texture (short, bright, off-beat chords) that you will use for contrast in arrangements.

[How to practice]
Tap the foot on the beat and count aloud. Play Strumming 14 — All Upstrokes at 60 BPM on one chord: the arm still swings down on every beat but passes above the strings. Keep the upstroke short: strike, then relax the fretting fingers on the following beat so the chord stops before the next up. Then replace the missed downstrokes with chucks. Move to a two-chord loop, then four chords, changing on beat 1 during the silent downbeat.
steps.successCriteria: You can play upstrokes only on the "ands" at 70–90 BPM over a four-chord loop for two minutes with the foot tapping steadily on the beat, the chord stopped before the next upstroke, and the tempo not drifting when the click is turned down.

steps.title: Shuffle and swing feel
steps.description:
[What it is]
Dividing the beat in three instead of two and playing the first and third part: a long-short, bouncing feel ("1 and-a 2 and-a"). Blues, early rock and roll, swing and many country and pop songs use it, and it changes where every upstroke falls: later than in straight eighths.

[Why it matters]
A shuffle played with straight eighths sounds wrong, and a straight song played with a shuffle sounds equally wrong; Andy Guitar's lesson stresses never mixing the two inside a song. Hearing and playing the difference is a basic requirement for accompanying blues and a large part of the classic rock repertoire. Triplets also sharpen your subdivision: three per beat is harder to feel than two.

[How to practice]
Play Timing — Triplets at 60 BPM on a single string, counting "1 trip-let" on each beat. Then strum only the first and third triplet: down on the beat, up on "let". Take a 12-bar blues in A (A, D, E) and play it as a shuffle with palm-muted downstrokes on the low strings and the up on the "let". Play the same progression straight, then shuffled, and record both to compare. Listen to a blues shuffle recording and play along.
steps.successCriteria: You can play a 12-bar blues in A as a shuffle at 60–80 BPM for the full form, with the upstroke landing on the third triplet rather than halfway, and switch between straight and shuffled versions of the same progression on request without mixing them.

lessons.title: How to Swing Strum Perfectly

steps.title: Switch subdivisions without changing tempo
steps.description:
[What it is]
Moving between quarter notes, eighths, triplets and sixteenths while the beat stays exactly where it is. The click does not change; only how many strokes you fit into each beat does.

[Why it matters]
Songs do this constantly: a verse in quarter notes, a pre-chorus in eighths, a chorus in sixteenths. Players who cannot switch either speed up when the strumming gets busier or slow down when it thins out. The skill is also the best check that the pulse really is inside you and not in your hand.

[How to practice]
Play Timing — Switch Subdivisions at 60 BPM: one bar of quarter notes, one of eighths, one of sixteenths, back down, on a single string. Count each subdivision aloud ("1, 2", "1 and", "1 e and a"). Then do the same with strums on one chord, and finally with a triplet bar in the sequence. Record with the click audible and listen for the beat drifting at the moment of the switch; that is where to slow down.
steps.successCriteria: You can play four bars cycling quarter notes, eighths, triplets and sixteenths on one chord at 60–80 BPM with the click audible and no drift at the switch points, and repeat it with the click on beats 2 and 4 only.

steps.title: Lock in with the drums
steps.description:
[What it is]
Playing with a drum track or backing track rather than a click, and placing your strums with the drums: downbeats with the kick, accents and chucks with the snare on 2 and 4, subdivisions with the hi-hat. The goal is that the guitar sounds like part of the drum kit.

[Why it matters]
This is what a rhythm guitarist is for in a band. Freddie Green said the guitar should never be heard by itself, only as part of the drums; Dave Isaacs teaches strumming as drumming. A part that is in time with a click but fights the drummer's accents still sounds wrong. Learning to hear the kit and match it is the difference between practising rhythm and playing it.

[How to practice]
Take a drum loop or backing track at 80–100 BPM. First only listen and clap the snare, then the hi-hat subdivision. Then play THE pattern with the accent on the snare and chucks where the snare falls. Turn the track down until you can barely hear it and keep playing; turn it up and check you are still together. Repeat the Metronome Gap Test at song tempos: the silent gap is now what happens between a drum fill and the next downbeat. Do the same with the click on beats 2 and 4 only.
steps.successCriteria: Playing THE pattern with a drum track at 80–100 BPM, your accents land with the snare and your downbeats with the kick for a full three-minute track, and when the track is muted for four bars you re-enter on the downbeat without an audible jump.

steps.title: Sixteenth notes and the funk scratch
steps.description:
[What it is]
Four strokes per beat, counted "1 e and a", with the hand moving down-up-down-up continuously and the fretting hand choosing which strokes ring and which are muted scratches. This is the Nile Rodgers approach: the right hand never stops, the left hand plays the rhythm.

[Why it matters]
Sixteenth-note strumming is the basis of funk, disco, R&B and a lot of modern pop, and even in slow ballads the hand often moves in sixteenths. It also makes accents on upstrokes, which Premier Guitar's Alex Nolan calls the biggest accent problem for guitarists, a trained skill instead of an accident.

[How to practice]
Mute the strings with the fretting hand and strum continuous sixteenths at 60 BPM, counting "1 e and a" aloud; keep the motion small and the wrist loose. Then play Strumming — Funk 16ths, which marks which strokes ring, which are muted and which are accented. Start by letting only the strokes on the beat ring and scratching the rest, then move the ringing stroke to the "and", then to the "a". Keep the tempo at 60–70 BPM; speed comes later.
steps.successCriteria: You can strum continuous sixteenths on muted strings at 70 BPM for two minutes with even spacing, then play the Funk 16ths pattern with the ringing strokes and accents in the right places, and place a single ringing stroke on the "e", "and" or "a" of a beat on request.

Funk Guitar Lesson - #1 16th Notes Rhythms - Chris Buono

steps.title: Read a chord chart and map the song
steps.description:
[What it is]
Taking a chord chart or lyric sheet and turning it into a map you can play from: the sections (intro, verse, chorus, bridge, outro), how many bars each has, how many beats each chord lasts, and where the changes fall relative to the lyrics.

[Why it matters]
A chart tells you the chords but rarely the timing. Players who skip the map get lost in the form, come in wrong after a chorus, or hold a chord for the wrong number of beats. Mapping a song is the first step of every song you will ever learn, and it turns the chord loops from the second phase into a real arrangement.

[How to practice]
Pick a song with three or four open chords. Listen with the chart and count bars per section; write the form as a list (intro 4, verse 8, chorus 8, and so on) and mark on the lyric sheet exactly which word each chord change falls on. Note where the pattern changes, where there are stops, and how the song ends. Then program the song's progression into Chord Practice — Pick Your Chords with the right number of beats per chord and play the form with the recording. Do this for three songs.
steps.successCriteria: For three songs you can write the complete form (sections, bar counts, beats per chord, where each change falls in the lyrics) from listening plus a chord chart, and play through the whole form with the recording without losing your place.

lessons.title: Song Structure Guitar Lesson | Guitar Tricks

steps.title: Choose and adapt a strum pattern for a song
steps.description:
[What it is]
Working out a pattern that fits a song instead of applying THE pattern to everything: matching the subdivision the drums play, the density of the original guitar part, the tempo and the section. A slow song may need sparse quarter notes; a chorus may need busy eighths with a push.

[Why it matters]
The same chords with the wrong pattern sound like a different, worse song. Adapting is the skill that separates "I know the chords" from "I can play the song", and it is what lets you accompany a singer who wants a song in a different tempo or feel from the record.

[How to practice]
For a song you have mapped, listen for the hi-hat subdivision and the guitar's density, and write a candidate pattern in counts. Try three versions: sparser, as heard, busier. Play Strumming 23 — Dense to Sparse to feel how density changes the energy inside one bar. Record each version with the recording and pick the one that sits best, then simplify it for the verse and thicken it for the chorus. Do this for three songs with different tempos.
steps.successCriteria: For three songs of different tempos you can propose a pattern in counts, play it with the recording, and explain why it fits (subdivision, density, section). A recording of you playing along sits with the drums and does not fight the original part.

steps.title: Sus-chord embellishments and fills
steps.description:
[What it is]
Decorating a chord you are holding by lifting or adding one finger in rhythm: Dsus2, Dsus4, Asus2, Asus4, Esus4, Cadd9, and walking bass notes between chords (G to C through the open A string, C to Am through the open A). The pattern stays the same; a finger moves on a specific count.

[Why it matters]
Embellishments are how rhythm guitarists keep two bars of one chord interesting without adding notes for the singer to fight. James Taylor's "Fire and Rain" and "Country Road" and hundreds of pop and worship songs rely on sus2 and sus4 movement, and a bass walk into the next chord is the simplest fill there is. This step also gives your fretting hand rhythmic independence: it moves on a count while the strum continues.

[How to practice]
Hold D and add the little finger for Dsus4 on the "and" of 2, lift it for D on 3, lift the first finger for Dsus2 on 4. Do the same with A and Asus4/Asus2, and with E and Esus4. Keep THE pattern going the whole time at 60–70 BPM. Then between G and C play the open A string on beat 4 as a walk-up. Program D, A, G and C into Chord Practice — Pick Your Chords and add one embellishment per chord.
steps.successCriteria: You can play a loop of D, A, G and C at 70 BPM with THE pattern and a sus2 or sus4 movement on a chosen count of every bar, plus a bass walk into at least one change, without the strum stopping or the tempo drifting.

steps.title: Section changes, intros and endings
steps.description:
[What it is]
Making the joins of a song sound intended: a build in the last bar of the verse into a louder chorus, a drop to a sparse pattern for a bridge, a clean start (count-in, first strum on beat 1) and a real ending (a final downbeat, a ring-out, or a stop on the last chord). Pattern, volume and sustain all change at the barline.

[Why it matters]
The joins are where accompaniment falls apart: the verse pattern leaks into the chorus, the ending trails off, the intro starts on a guess. A song with clean sections and a decisive ending sounds finished even when the middle is simple. This also prepares you to lead a band, where the guitarist often signals the changes.

[How to practice]
Play Strumming 30 — Slow to Fast, which builds from sparse to dense inside one bar, and use it as the last bar of a verse. Build a verse-chorus form from a song you mapped: eight bars soft and sparse, a build bar, eight bars loud with THE pattern, then a bridge of four bars of half notes, and repeat. Practise two endings: a ring-out on the final chord after a count-in of "1, 2, 3, 4", and a stop on the last beat 1. Start every run with a spoken count-in.
steps.successCriteria: You can play a verse-chorus-bridge form at 80 BPM with a clearly different pattern and volume in each section, a build into every chorus, a spoken count-in before the first strum and a decisive ending, and a listener can name the sections from the guitar alone.

steps.title: Learn a song by ear
steps.description:
[What it is]
Working out a simple song's rhythm part from the recording without a chart: finding the key by matching the bass or the final chord, hearing when the chord changes (counting bars), identifying whether each chord is major or minor, and copying the strumming by ear.

[Why it matters]
Charts are often wrong or missing, and a band rehearsal rarely waits for you to find one. Hearing where chords change and how the guitar strums is the fastest way to learn any song and the skill that keeps improving for the rest of your playing life. It ties together everything from counting bars to writing patterns in counts.

[How to practice]
Choose a song with three or four chords. Find the key by humming the note the song rests on and matching it on the low E string. Count bars aloud while listening and mark every chord change. For each chord, try the diatonic candidates in that key (in G: G, C, D, Em, Am) and keep the one that matches the bass. Write the pattern in counts, then play along. Use Play by Ear — Easy daily to sharpen pitch matching. Do one song per week.
steps.successCriteria: You can take a three- or four-chord song you have never seen a chart for, find the key, write its form and chords from listening in under 30 minutes, and play along with the recording using a pattern that matches.

lessons.title: How to Identify Chord Progressions by Ear - Music Theory for Guitarists Unit 2 Lesson 3

steps.title: Play a whole song with the track
steps.description:
[What it is]
A complete run-through of one song from the count-in to the ending with the recording or a backing track: right chords, a pattern that fits, changes on time, section dynamics, no stopping and no restarting when something goes wrong.

[Why it matters]
Practising sections is not the same as playing a song. Endurance, memory of the form and recovering from a mistake without dropping the beat only get trained by playing from start to finish. This is the first checkpoint of what the roadmap promised: a usable rhythm part.

[How to practice]
Use a song you mapped and adapted. Play it with the recording three times per session, keeping a tally of stops, late changes and lost places. When something goes wrong, keep strumming muted strings and re-enter at the next section; never restart. Track your time on the song in the Songs library so the practice is logged. When a run has no stops, play it with the track turned down to a whisper, then with a drum loop only.
steps.successCriteria: You can play one complete song with the recording, count-in to ending, three times in a row without stopping or restarting, with every section in the right place and no more than two late changes per run, and once more with only a drum loop.

steps.title: Tempo range and stamina
steps.description:
[What it is]
Playing your song and its pattern comfortably across a range of tempos: 15 percent slower than the record, at the record's tempo, and 10 percent faster; and keeping the strumming even for a whole song without the arm tightening.

[Why it matters]
Singers ask for songs slower or faster, drummers push, and nerves speed everything up on stage. A part that only works at one tempo is fragile. Playing slower than the record also exposes rushed changes and uneven strums that the faster tempo hides, and stamina keeps the last chorus as clean as the first.

[How to practice]
Find the song's tempo. Play Strumming 31 — Skip the Last Up (a common pop pattern) with the metronome at the slow, target and fast tempos in one session, one minute each, checking that the strum stays even and the pendulum motion stays the same size. Then play the whole song at each tempo with a click. Between runs, shake the arm out; if the wrist tightens, drop the tempo and reduce the stroke size. Keep a log of the highest tempo at which the song is clean.
steps.successCriteria: You can play your song clean at the record's tempo, at 15 percent slower and at 10 percent faster with a click, each in one run without stopping, and the strumming in the final chorus of each run is as even as in the first verse.

steps.title: Record, review and fix
steps.description:
[What it is]
Recording a full run with the click or track audible, listening back with a checklist, and deciding what to fix: early or late relative to the click, uneven volume, chords not clean on the first strum, sections that do not change, endings that trail off. Then one focused fix per session.

[Why it matters]
While you play you cannot hear yourself the way a listener does; most rhythm problems (rushing the chorus, dragging after a change) are invisible from inside. A recording and a checklist make them concrete, and fixing one thing at a time is how professionals rehearse. It is also the last check before playing with other people.

[How to practice]
Record with your phone, click or track clearly audible. Listen once without playing, marking every place you are ahead of or behind the click, then every dirty change, then the dynamics. Pick the single biggest issue and drill only that section for the session, then re-record. Use Rhythm Training — Medium as a warm-up: it scores your placement of eighth notes and rests so you can see whether you tend to rush or drag.
steps.successCriteria: You have three recordings of the same song from different sessions, each with a written list of issues, and the last recording shows the first list's biggest problem fixed: no section is consistently ahead of or behind the click, and every chord is clean on its first strum.

steps.title: Play with other people
steps.description:
[What it is]
Playing your rhythm part with at least one other person (another guitarist, a singer, a drummer, a bassist, or a play-along video with a real band) without a click: listening, keeping the beat when the other person wobbles, leaving room, and following a count-in.

[Why it matters]
Everything so far has been against a perfect clock. People are not perfect clocks. A rhythm guitarist has to hold the tempo when the singer rushes, stay out of the way of the vocal, and lock with a drummer's feel rather than a click. There is no substitute for doing it, and it is what "accompaniment" means.

[How to practice]
Find one person and one song you both know. Agree the tempo with a spoken count-in and play it through three times. Between runs talk about one thing: who was rushing, whether the guitar was too loud under the vocal, whether the changes were together. If there are two guitarists, split into a sparse and a busy part. Record the session. If nobody is available, use full-band play-along videos with no click and treat them the same way.
steps.successCriteria: You have played a full song with at least one other person, without a click, three times through with a count-in, and a recording shows the tempo held steady and the guitar sitting under the vocal or with the drums rather than fighting them.

lessons.title: Do THIS when playing with another guitarist

steps.title: Your rhythm part, start to finish
steps.description:
[What it is]
The final performance: one song of your choice with three or more chords, played complete as a rhythm part you arranged yourself: mapped form, a pattern chosen for the song, sections with different dynamics and sustain, at least one embellishment or push, a clean count-in and ending, at the record's tempo, recorded in one take with a backing track or another musician.

[Why it matters]
This is the promise of the roadmap made checkable. Every earlier step exists so that this recording is possible: pulse, clean chords, changes on time, patterns with rests and pushes, muting, accents, dynamics, and a form you can hold in your head. When it is done you have a part you could play in a band tomorrow.

[How to practice]
Choose the song and write a one-page arrangement: form with bar counts, pattern per section, volume per section, where the chucks, palm mutes or sus movements go, how it starts and how it ends. Rehearse sections, then whole runs, using the review checklist from the previous step. Record the take. Then do it again with a second song in a different feel (a shuffle, sixteenth-note strumming or a palm-muted rock part) so the skills are not tied to one song.

[What you can do now]
You keep a pulse without a click, play the common open chords cleanly and change them at song tempo, read and write strum patterns, use rests, accents, palm mutes and chucks on purpose, play straight, shuffled and sixteenth-note feels, and carry a whole song with a band or a recording.
steps.successCriteria: You have a one-take recording of a complete song, count-in to ending, with a backing track or another musician at the record's tempo, in which the sections are audibly different, the changes are on time, the pattern fits the song and there are no stops; plus a second song in a different feel.
